title: Binary Indexed Tree
html:
A binary indexed tree (Fenwick tree) supports prefix queries and point updates over a fixed-size array in O(log n) each, using a single array of n + 1 integers and a handful of lines of code. It is the lightweight alternative to a segment tree for sums, counts and XORs.

Binary indexed tree (BIT, Fenwick tree) — an array BIT[1..n] in which BIT[i] stores the sum of the i & −i elements of the input ending at position i (1-based). Prefix sums and updates both walk O(log n) entries by repeatedly clearing or adding the lowest set bit of the index.

It is used for a fixed input array with many operations of two kinds: a prefix operation — sum, product, XOR, OR, count — and updating a value. It is stored as a plain array, but the idea behind the indices is a tree. It needs O(n log n) preprocessing (O(n) with a trick) and Θ(n) auxiliary space.

Example

Input: arr = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60]; getSum(2); getSum(4)
Output: 60 150
Input: update(2, 35); getSum(2); getSum(4)
Output: 65 155

rangeSum(i, j) = prefixSum(j) − prefixSum(i − 1)

Three approaches to prefix sum + update

getSum(i) returns arr[0] + … + arr[i]; update(i, x) sets arr[i] = x. Both operations are frequent and interleaved.

MethodgetSum(i)update(i, x)SpaceCode
1 — simple: loop from 0 to iO(n)O(1) — arr[i] = xO(1)trivial
2 — prefix-sum array: pre[i]O(1)O(n) — add diff to pre[i..n−1]O(n)trivial
3 — segment treeO(log n)O(log n)≈ 4nthree recursive functions
Binary indexed treeO(log n)O(log n)n + 1two short loops

Methods 1 and 2 each make one operation linear; with a mixed workload the average cost is O(n) per operation. The segment tree fixes that but is a comparatively heavy piece of code. The BIT gets the same O(log n) for both operations with less memory and about ten lines.

Limitation

Unlike a segment tree, a BIT works only for operations that have an inverse: rangeSum(i, j) = getSum(j) − getSum(i−1) needs subtraction. Prefix min or max cannot be undone, so range-min queries need a segment tree.

The idea: every prefix is a sum of powers of two

Any positive integer is a sum of distinct powers of two: 14 = 8 + 4 + 2. So a prefix of length 14 can be split into three blocks of lengths 8, 4 and 2, and if the sum of each block is pre-computed, getSum needs three additions instead of fourteen. The BIT stores exactly these blocks: entry i (1-based) is responsible for the last i & −i elements ending at i.

The i & -i trick: isolating the lowest set bit

−i in two's complement is ~i + 1: flip every bit, then add one. Flipping turns the trailing zeros of i into ones and the lowest 1 into 0; adding one carries through those ones and stops exactly at that position. The result shares only that one bit with i, so i & −i is the lowest set bit as a power of two.

ExpressionEffectUsed by
i -= i & -iclear the lowest set bit → jump to the parent blockgetSum (walk towards 0)
i += i & -iadd the lowest set bit → jump to the next entry whose block contains iupdate (walk towards n)

getSum: prefix sum

To get the sum of arr[0..i], convert to the 1-based BIT index i + 1 and keep adding BIT[i] while clearing the lowest set bit. Every step removes one 1 bit, so there are at most log₂ n steps.

Example

getSum(4): i = 5 (101) → add BIT[5] = 50, i = 4 (100) → add BIT[4] = 100, i = 0 → stop. Result 150.

update: change one value

The first parameter is an index of arr. Compute diff = x − arr[i], store the new value, convert to the 1-based index and add diff to every BIT entry whose block contains i — these are reached by adding the lowest set bit each time until the index exceeds n.

Construction and the complete program

Idea

Build the BIT by starting from all zeros and calling update(i, arr[i]) for every element — n updates of O(log n) each. The program below builds the tree for [10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60], answers prefix and range sums, performs an update and queries again.

Time O(log n) per getSum / update; O(n log n) constructionSpace O(n)
Linear construction

Construction can be O(n): copy arr into BIT[1..n], then for i = 1..n add BIT[i] into BIT[i + (i & −i)] if that index is ≤ n. Every entry pushes its total to the one parent block that contains it — one pass, no logarithm.

Pitfall

Two off-by-one traps: the BIT is 1-based (so arr[i] lives at i + 1, and BIT[0] is never used), and update must use the difference against the stored arr[i], not the new value — unless you are adding to an element rather than setting it, in which case the diff is the amount added and no arr copy is needed.

Interview Q&A

Explain i & -i.

In two's complement −i = ~i + 1. Negating flips all bits, and the +1 carries through the trailing ones, stopping at the position of i's lowest set bit. That bit is the only one set in both i and −i, so i & −i is exactly the lowest set bit (a power of two). In a BIT it is the length of the block entry i is responsible for.

Why is getSum O(log n)?

Every iteration clears one set bit of the index (i -= i & -i). A number below n has at most ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 set bits, so the loop runs that many times at most. update is symmetric: i += i & -i increases the position of the lowest set bit each time, so it also takes O(log n) steps to exceed n.

BIT vs segment tree?

Same O(log n) for point update and prefix/range query. BIT: n + 1 memory, ~10 lines, faster constants; but only for invertible operations (sum, XOR, count) and point updates. Segment tree: any associative operation (min, max, gcd), range updates via lazy propagation, ≈ 4n memory, more code.

How do you do a range update + point query with a BIT?

Store the differences: to add v to [l, r] do add(l, v) and add(r + 1, −v); a point query at i is then prefixSum(i). Range update + range query needs two BITs. Both tricks rely on the sum being invertible.

Name two classic BIT applications beyond prefix sums.

Counting inversions in O(n log n): scan left to right and query how many previously seen values are greater. Order statistics / k-th smallest among the inserted values with a binary search over the BIT (O(log² n) or O(log n) with bit-walking). Both treat the BIT as a dynamic frequency table.
